item.title: Log10x App - v1.1.7 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
* Field conditions after `tx` match key\=value text, such as `status=600`, syslog's `uid=0` or `EventCode=4624`: the fields of an expanded event are the ones Splunk extracts from the original line, key\=value pairs and JSON alike, and no others. * Dates expand as written when a day, hour, minute or second has no leading zero, such as syslog's `Sep 5 00:14:52`. * A timestamp that was already an epoch number expands as that number. * A `tx` search with nothing to narrow on no longer highlights the whole of every event. * After upgrading, run `index=tenx_dml sourcetype=tenx_dml_raw_json earliest=0 | sendalert tenx_dml_to_kv` once, so that templates stored by an earlier version take the date changes.


Short Description:
Send Splunk the logs that sampling and filters keep out to fit the license, on that same license. Compact events take a fraction of the volume and expand back byte-identical at search time; classic dashboards keep their SPL, and one command covers the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API.


Description:
With the Log10x App, Splunk can index compact log events and still search, chart and alert on the original lines. The 10x Receiver stores each event as a template hash plus the values that change, so a stream of repeated patterns takes less of the license. On the OpenTelemetry demo, Splunk's license meter counted 63.91% fewer bytes, encoded events and templates included, and every line expanded back byte-identical with the Receiver settings in the installation steps (measurement: https://github.com/log-10x/benchmarks/tree/main/splunk-license). The same license then holds more: sources that were sampled, filtered or kept out of Splunk to stay under the limit can come back, or the license can be smaller. Classic dashboards keep their SPL: the browser sends each panel's search to the app, which rewrites it on the server. From the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API, a search is wrapped in the tx command (tenxsearch also works). An alert created in the app's Compile Alert view is compiled once into a native saved search, so the scheduler runs no Python. NOT, OR, groups, phrases, field conditions, and values such as IP addresses and hostnames behave as they do on the original data. The 10x Receiver produces compact events, and it is free on up to 10 nodes (https://www.log10x.com/pricing). No sign-up is required to evaluate it: with no license token it runs the full product for 30 days on up to 10 nodes, air-gapped, and a free license removes the time limit (https://doc.log10x.com/manage/license/). The app itself is open source under the MIT license.

item.title: Cisco Enterprise Networking Add-on for Splunk - v4.0.60 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
* **Consistent syslog port instructions:** Removed competing port recommendations from forms and setup guidance. Firewall and troubleshooting examples now follow SD-WAN TCP/TLS 9514 and UDP 514, ISE 9515, and Cyber Vision 9516. The optional SD-WAN receiver-side redirect uses UDP 9514 while senders continue targeting UDP 514. Existing inputs are unchanged. * **Cyber Vision secure syslog:** Added TLS (Secure SysLog) on suggested TCP 9516 with a required receiver-readiness confirmation. The guide covers Cyber Vision TCP + TLS, approved P12 certificate import, matching receiver trust and delivery validation. Existing TCP/UDP inputs are unchanged; live certificate trust and encrypted delivery require deployment validation. * **Dedicated syslog port suggestions:** New inputs suggest SD-WAN TCP or TLS 9514/UDP 514, ISE TLS, TCP or UDP 9515, and Cyber Vision TLS, TCP or UDP 9516. Cyber Vision now starts with TCP and a populated port. Defaults are editable; saved inputs are unchanged. The UI, firewall examples and guide use this product port table consistently. * **ISE sender configuration reminder:** The Syslog form highlights Comply to RFC 3164, matching protocol and port, supported message length, and category assignment. The guide explains delimiter escaping, save/reopen confirmation and fresh-event validation. This setting does not reconstruct missing JSON or establish the cause of a malformed payload. * **TLS syslog input saves:** Sends literal `SSL=true` to the native REST handler for TLS and omits the unnecessary flag for plain TCP. Declares persisted metadata under the platform's native TLS specification, avoiding a custom modular-input classification during Cloud review. Upgrades preserve existing local inputs; invalid plain TCP entries still require correction, and receiver certificates/trust and an enabled TLS handshake remain separate prerequisites. * **ISE alarm severity:** Maps ISE's `CRITICAL` alarm level to `severity=critical`, including retained events, while preserving existing mappings and raw syslog. This is a search-time correction and does not require reindexing or repair malformed API content. * **ISE probe-derived endpoint context (experimental):** `ENDPOINTS_DATA` adds `NAD_ADDRESS`, `ENDPOINT_SOURCE`, `LOGICAL_PROFILE`, and `ENDPOINT_NAME` using bounded Oracle projections. Corrected an unsupported zero-separator requirement that could reject otherwise extractable values. New `ise_probe_diagnostics` explains missing keys, duplicate keys, incomplete headers/values, invalid lengths and unsupported values instead of exposing only `unavailable`. Full inventory collection retains endpoints without RADIUS authentication; raw `PROBE_DATA` remains excluded. Field matching is heuristic and can match embedded field-name text; use the FullReport workflow as the primary NAD source until native format, accuracy, coverage, freshness and largest-cluster performance are validated. * **ISE pxGrid connection tests:** Test Connection now uses the saved or supplied pxGrid client password/certificate for one read-only session service lookup and validates the first provider's HTTPS/8910 URL and trusted hostname using the collector's rules. Missing credentials, rejected access, unavailable services, unsafe/untrusted provider locations, TLS failures and inconclusive responses fail the test with actionable guidance. Added support for Cisco's documented `/pxgrid/mnt/sd` Session Directory route, preserving the node allowlist and rejection of unrelated paths. The check has a ten-second request/deadline budget, a 64 KiB response cap and no automatic retries. It never creates, activates or approves a client. REST and Data Connect results remain visible; individual dataset/Guest/Monitoring permissions and indexed delivery still require collector verification. Password dots are preservation placeholders, not proof of a stored secret. * **ISE pxGrid provider routing:** Session collection accepts the Session Directory route; IP-to-SGT binding collection discovers the SXP provider and sends `getBindings` to its explicitly trusted HTTPS URL instead of the control node. Unrelated provider hosts, unsupported paths and redirects remain rejected. Successful account service discovery does not prove per-service `gets` authorization or provider data access; verify the selected collectors' first polls. * **Illustrated SD-WAN NetFlow guide:** Added customer walkthroughs for v9/HSL and v10/Unified Logging with Manager and Splunk screenshots, separate canary acceptance, HF/downstream verification, troubleshooting and collector-wide capacity measurement. Kept SUL release/policy/resource boundaries and ordinary cFlowd distinct. * **HF validation:** Local configuration readiness is separate from downstream indexed delivery. Forwarding-only hosts default to no indexed-data searches. Detected local or available downstream search can suggest local verification; manual choices remain available. Local searches preserve generating-command syntax and zero results remain unverified. Data Collection Health explains downstream search requirements. Cisco NetFlow package discovery uses the short NetFlow catalog query. * **Search visibility detection:** NetFlow setup and Data Collection Health distinguish downstream search configured, local search only, and search visibility unknown. Local metadata suggests a search location and shows observed peer status and last-check time; manual choices survive refresh. Peer configuration does not prove index access or data arrival. Detection is bounded and launches no search jobs. * **NetFlow listener reset:** Replaced deletion of package-provided Stream stanzas with a verified disabled override and receiver-0-only reset. Other configured NetFlow receivers block reset; unrelated settings, routing, HEC and indexed data remain intact. Errors leave completion unverified. Restart remains operator-controlled. * **Save and host context:** Listener saves change only modified shared settings and verify readback. Rejected input updates identify partial saves without rendering raw server error pages. Search visibility also shows the host and reported Splunk roles, separately from search access or delivery proof. * **Health dashboard layout:** Deployment context and search visibility appear below the tabs and filters in a section collapsed by default. The heading retains the search visibility status; expand it for deployment details and refresh. Product cards now show one status combining freshness and collection findings: partial or unverified coverage is amber; persistent failures are red. **View details** includes affected inputs and expected sourcetypes alongside freshness evidence. Multi-sourcetype report lists remain complete, and dialogs stay above the sidebar on narrower screens. * **Support bundle source and streaming:** Search heads and hosts with an available downstream peer default to indexed logs; forwarding-only hosts without that search path default to local TA files. The source remains selectable. Full exports compress logs as they are processed, removing the cumulative uncompressed-size cutoff while retaining the 50 MiB compressed, one-million-event and five-minute limits. Versioned worker assets avoid stale support-export code after upgrades; refresh open pages. * **Local bundle diagnostics:** Failed local file reads show their HTTP status when available. A ZIP with no log events and unavailable log sections is explicitly labeled configuration-only rather than showing a successful log collection message. * **Support bundle recovery:** When local file collection is unavailable, the dialog explains how to install the TA on a search head with access to the HF’s forwarded TA logs in `_internal` and generate an indexed bundle there. Configuration-only or partial downloads remain clearly identified. * **Compact support diagnostics:** Indexed exports can include full-window counts with up to 250 warning/error and 250 other log samples per section, shortening each sample to 8,192 characters and recording omitted counts. Full indexed and bounded local modes remain available; local file tails retain at most 10,000 latest matching records per file and disclose omissions. An offline verifier checks archive structure, counts and CRCs without extracting log files. * **SD-WAN collection-path reference:** Application Setup now shows which data comes from ordinary text syslog, HSL/NetFlow v9, Unified Logging/IPFIX v10, or Manager REST inputs, and when each sourcetype is expected. HSL flow records remain separate from text syslog.


Short Description:
Collect and normalize data from Cisco Catalyst Center (DNA Center, DNAC), Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN / SDWAN (vManage), Cisco ISE, Cisco Cyber Vision (CyberVision), and supported Cisco network devices. The included User Guide covers installation, deployment, configuration, validation, and troubleshooting.


Description:
Cisco Enterprise Networking Add-on for Splunk, also known as the Cisco Catalyst Add-on, collects and normalizes API, syslog, and NetFlow data from Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center, DNAC), Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN and Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager (SDWAN, formerly vManage), Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE), and Cisco Cyber Vision (CyberVision). The add-on includes an in-product User Guide with current installation, deployment, configuration, validation, and troubleshooting instructions. item.title: Log Continuity Manager for Splunk - v1.2.4 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Version 1.2.4 Reliability, Locking and Dashboard Improvements \- Improved runtime lock contention handling across notification, Mass Interruption, status and history workflows. \- Notification preparation, email delivery and notification outcome operations now use bounded runtime lock acquisition instead of failing immediately on short-lived contention. \- Added safe owner-fenced lock release behavior to prevent an older lock owner from affecting a newer lock. \- Active runtime lock records remain immutable and cannot be overwritten by competing writers. \- Added enhanced runtime lock diagnostics for: \- contention \- retry scheduling \- successful retry \- retry-budget exhaustion \- release duration \- non-contention REST/KV failures \- Improved diagnostic visibility through Splunk-managed python.log telemetry. \- Added safe classification for non-contention failures without exposing credentials, request bodies or sensitive payloads. \- Improved UTF-8 and Unicode handling across target, policy and persistence workflows. \- Valid Turkish UTF-8 characters are supported in fields such as Owner, Description and policy metadata. \- Malformed or unsupported text encoding is rejected safely before persistence. \- Fixed a Quick Add issue where successfully created targets could incorrectly be reported as blocked. \- Replaced the legacy Log Interruption Health Dashboard with a new Dashboard Studio Operations Center while preserving the existing dashboard view ID and navigation compatibility. \- Added Operations Overview and Target Investigation views with improved severity, health, monitoring-type and target-level visibility. Validation \- 487 Python regression tests passed. \- Runtime lock, contention, notification lifecycle, Unicode and diagnostic tests passed. \- JavaScript tests and syntax checks passed. \- XML and configuration validation passed. \- Dashboard Studio structure and references validated. \- Live LAB validation confirmed successful bounded retries under runtime contention without lock ownership errors after startup stabilization. Compatibility \- No KV Store schema changes. \- No Search Head Cluster replication changes. \- No scheduler cadence changes. \- Existing monitoring targets remain compatible. \- Existing notification, recovery, maintenance, redundancy and Mass Interruption workflows are preserved.


Short Description:
Log Continuity Manager provides KV Store-backed log interruption monitoring, recovery tracking, notification workflows, Mass Interruption policies and Dashboard Studio-based operational visibility for Splunk Enterprise environments.


Description:
Log Continuity Manager for Splunk helps teams detect, manage and investigate log ingestion interruptions across monitored hosts, indexes, sources and sourcetypes. The app supports target-based continuity monitoring, interruption detection, recovery tracking, maintenance and redundancy-aware handling, and operational dashboards for monitoring status and history. Version 1.2.1 adds Mass Interruption monitoring with Host Count and Percentage thresholds, scoped policies for host_index, host_index_source and host_index_sourcetype targets, interruption/reminder/recovery email notifications, notification delivery visibility, KV Store-backed runtime state, and improved Search Head Cluster readiness. The app is designed for Splunk Enterprise environments where continuous log visibility and rapid identification of ingestion gaps are operationally important.

item.title: Hurricane Labs Add-on for Anthropic Compliance API - v1.2.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
UPGRADE NOTES \- Activity events now carry a CIM verb in action (read, uploaded, shared, commented, created, updated, deleted, acl_modified, modified, pending). action\=success now means a successful sign-in or sign-out only. Saved searches and alerts that filter activity events on action\=success will match far fewer events; filter on type or signature instead. Accelerated Authentication, Change and Data Access summaries keep the old values until they are rebuilt. \- Org-user records are no longer counted as logins in CIM Authentication. \- Records arrive about 5 minutes later: the inputs hold back the newest 5 minutes so records the API lists a few seconds late are still collected. COLLECTION \- Activity Feed: events the API lists late are no longer lost (\~1% of events). Events the API lists twice are written once. The first-run backfill saves its place after every page and resumes where it stopped. Incremental runs catch up in one run. Timeouts, connection errors and HTTP 5xx are retried. \- Chats: later runs write only new messages instead of whole threads. A chat whose messages can't be fetched is retried on later runs, and the alert flags it after 3 failed runs. A run that fails partway resends messages rather than skipping any. \- Chats and Apps: a host clock running fast can't make them skip records. The Apps checkpoint is saved atomically. Retry-After is handled safely. OPERATIONS \- New alert, "Anthropic Compliance - Input failing" (disabled by default): fires when an input's runs fail, or when the Chats input gives up on a chat's messages. \- An API key with stray characters can no longer leak into the logs. \- claudechats rows get the right \_time on Splunk 9.x. \- The add-on's own logs are indexed under their own sourcetypes. \- Unused OpenTelemetry/gRPC libraries are no longer bundled; the package is about half the size. CONNECTIONS \- Per-account API Base URL and CA Bundle Path, for non-default endpoints (for example, FedRAMP) and TLS-inspecting proxies. \- Requests never follow redirects, so the API key only goes to the configured host. CIM AND DASHBOARDS \- Failed logins reach CIM Authentication for the first time. Only sign-in and sign-out activity carries the authentication tag. \- Chat, file, project and artifact activity is in CIM Data Access for the first time (needs CIM add-on 4.20.0 or later). \- Change events carry the change and audit tags, a Change verb in action, and their outcome in status. \- object and object_category name the most specific thing an event is about; user is filled for SCIM and system changes; dest reflects the account's API host. Org, group and project context is searchable as org_id, org_name, group_id, group_name and project_id. \- Fixed dashboard panels: Admin Change Events Over Time, Authentication Activity, the Org column and Group Membership. Full details: README.txt in the add-on, section "Release notes".


Short Description:
Splunk Technology Add-on that ingests data from the Anthropic Compliance API for audit, eDiscovery, DLP, insider-risk, and governance use cases.

item.title: endoflife.ai EOL Risk - v0.1.0 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
0.1.0, first release. The `eollookup` streaming search command (cycles and full patch versions, split-line refusal with candidates), the EOL Risk Overview dashboard, four example reports (none scheduled), a setup page that stores the API key in Splunk's encrypted credential store, and the `endoflife_products` name-to-slug lookup with the `endoflife_normalize` macro. The lookup is a snapshot taken when this version was built. Bundles the Splunk Enterprise SDK for Python 2.1.1. Verified on Splunk Enterprise 10.6 (Python 3.13); `commands.conf` declares Python 3.9 and 3.13.


Short Description:
Add end-of-life dates, support status, EOL Risk Scores and CISA KEV exposure to the software inventory you already have in Splunk.


Description:
Most inventories can tell you what is installed. Few can tell you what the maker has stopped patching. This app adds that answer to the software and operating-system inventory you already collect in Splunk. The eollookup search command takes a product and a version from each row and adds: - whether the version is still supported, close to its end, or past end of life - the end-of-life date, with days remaining or days past - the EOL Risk Score (0 to 100) and its letter grade - whether the product has an entry in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog - where the date comes from, as a link you can open Full patch versions work: 18.19.0 is answered for the Node.js 18 line, 8.6 for RHEL 8. When a build could belong to more than one support line (SQL Server service packs, Firefox standard and ESR) the app does not pick one. It says so and lists the candidates. Nothing is guessed. Included: - eollookup, a streaming search command that batches lookups, so a search over many hosts makes few API calls - an overview dashboard: past end of life, ending within 180 days, past end of life with a CISA KEV entry, and rows that could not be matched - four example reports, none scheduled - a setup page that stores your API key in Splunk's encrypted credential store Coverage is 700+ products: operating systems, databases, language runtimes, frameworks, network and security appliances. Every date names its source. What leaves your environment: product names and version strings, sent over HTTPS to api.endoflife.ai when the command runs. No host names, users, IP addresses or event data. The app works without an API key at the anonymous limits until November 16, 2026; from then the API needs a key for every lookup. A free key (150 requests a day, no expiry) is enough to evaluate it: https://endoflife.ai/api#free-key. Keys and their limits are published at https://endoflife.ai/api.

item.title: Webtools Add-on Professional Edition - v4.0.4 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Version 4.0.4: **Client certificate without key file** — `clientcert=` works on its own again (any 3.1.2+ failed with `Could not find the TLS key file, invalid path: None` unless you also passed a key param). Separate cert+key still works via `certkey=`. **POST payload fidelity** — the `data=` option is no longer auto-JSON-parsed: it is transmitted exactly as entered and `curl_data_payload` (debug) echoes your original JSON instead of a Python dict repr (`'single quotes'`). Tip: single-quote the option value (`data='{"key": "value"}'`) to protect nested `"` from Splunk's search parser. Fixed `%3D` format crash in `splunkpasswdname`/`splunkpasswdcontext` password lookup. Restored 2.x SSL default: off-cloud instances default `verifyssl=false`; Splunk Cloud still always verifies. Pass `verifyssl=true` to opt back in. Internal password-store lookup no longer requires a trusted cert on the management port.


Short Description:
Enterprise network operations and security suite adding 14 custom search commands to Splunk: curl, openssl, dig, ping, trace, whois, scp, sftp, ftp, telnet, file, speedtest, letsencrypt, and urlencode for network diagnostics, security testing, and web service integration.


Description:
TA-webtools-pro is a comprehensive enterprise network operations and security suite that extends Splunk with 14 powerful custom search commands. This professional-grade addon enables security analysts, threat hunters, and DevOps teams to perform critical network and security operations directly from Splunk searches without leaving the platform. The addon addresses the critical need for integrated network diagnostics, security testing, and web service interaction within the Splunk ecosystem. Instead of switching between multiple tools or writing custom scripts, users can execute HTTP requests, DNS queries, cryptographic operations, network connectivity tests, file transfers, and domain lookups using familiar Splunk search syntax. Key capabilities include: HTTP/HTTPS requests via curl, cryptographic operations with OpenSSL (hashing, encryption, key generation, TLS certificate validation), DNS lookups with dig, network connectivity testing with ping and telnet, network path analysis with traceroute, domain registration queries with WHOIS, secure file transfers via SCP/SFTP/FTP, file reading from local and remote sources, network speed testing, and automated SSL certificate management with Let's Encrypt. Perfect for security operations centers (SOC), threat hunting teams, DevOps engineers, and network administrators who need to enrich security events with external data, validate network connectivity, test API endpoints, verify TLS certificates, perform domain reputation checks, and execute forensic investigations - all within Splunk.

item.title: PolySwarm Malware Reputation and Sandbox - v1.4.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Version 1.4.0 carries the 1.3.0 changes as well, which were never published separately, so an upgrade from 1.2.1 lands both sets at once. NEW: three saved searches an AI agent can call by name. PolySwarm Indicator Lookup takes one indicator and returns one row. PolySwarm Indicator Lookup with Attribution adds malware family and actor at up to double the cost. PolySwarm Quota Remaining reports what is left and spends no indicator quota. They exist so an AI agent reaching Splunk through an MCP server can use this app without an administrator registering a custom tool or editing an allowlist. All three ship disabled. Two of them spend a metered request every time something dispatches them, so turning them on is a deliberate act: Settings, Searches reports and alerts, with the App filter and the Owner filter both set to All, then Enable from the row's Edit menu. They carry no schedule, so enabling one starts nothing. NEW FIELD: polyswarm_status, on both lookup searches, reading answered, not_found, refused or error. A lookup that failed used to be indistinguishable from a value PolySwarm has no record of. It is not any more. NEW FIELD: daily_api_metered, on the account row. An unmetered plan reports a daily limit of zero beside a remaining count that reads as nothing left and means no cap. This field says which it is. FIXED: the command now reads its credential and its configuration in this app's namespace. Running polyswarmsearch from another app, the Search app included, failed with an error saying no API key was stored. That is the first thing many customers tried. FIXED: a missing API key reported a Python file path and a line number. Every command now names the setup page instead. CHANGED, AND IT CHANGES A PUBLISHED FIELD: PolyScore is no longer published for a URL, a domain or an address. The column is still there and it is empty on those rows. The platform returns the same score for every URL artifact whatever the detection engines reported, so a convicted host read as benign. Read the verdict and the detection counts for those indicator types. If you alert, rank or report on PolyScore for URL, domain or address indicators, review those rules before upgrading. CHANGED: certificate verification on the app's connection to splunkd is now an administrator setting, and it ships off. Splunk ships an environment variable that disables verification outright, so the setting makes the choice visible rather than assumed. RENAMED: the app is now PolySwarm Malware Reputation and Sandbox. The app id, the directory, every command, every field name and every saved object are unchanged, so an upgrade carries everything over. Tested on Splunk Enterprise 10.6.0.5. Supported on 9.4 through 10.6 and on Splunk Cloud Platform.


Short Description:
PolySwarm malware reputation, sandbox detonation and file reputation for Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud. Hash lookup and IOC enrichment for MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, URLs, domains and IP addresses: crowd-sourced verdicts from many engines, malware family attribution, an opt-in threat intel feed, a matching search and three saved searches an AI agent can call.


Description:
PolySwarm Malware Reputation and Sandbox integrates crowd-sourced malware threat intelligence into Splunk by enriching indicators of compromise, or IOCs, with verdicts derived from multiple detection engines. It is a file reputation and hash lookup source for the SOC: the app processes MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 hashes, URLs, domains and IP addresses found in Splunk events, annotating them with verdicts, detection counts and malware family attribution sourced from the PolySwarm platform. It extracts and refangs indicators from raw text fields within the search head environment, at no cost and with no API key, and submits URLs to a cloud-based sandbox for behavioral analysis. The app operates entirely on the search head tier and relies on a key-value store to cache verdict data, track sandbox task state, and maintain modular input checkpoints. Enrichment occurs through five specialized search commands that query the PolySwarm API: the indicators being looked up are sent to PolySwarm, and nothing else from the deployment is transmitted. A local verdict cache means a repeated indicator costs nothing, and every metered request carries an explicit ceiling. Search heads that reach the internet through a proxy can route this traffic through it, with credentials held in encrypted storage and certificate verification on the PolySwarm connection always enforced. Events tagged with the polyswarm:artifact source type represent threat intel pulled from the PolySwarm feed and from sandbox task results, and each one carries the artifact's MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-256 so it can be matched against events however your own sources log a digest. Four saved searches ship and all four ship disabled. PolySwarm Indicator Match correlates the indexed feed against your own events and carries the verdict, detection counts, family attribution and report link through to the alert, so an analyst sees why a match matters rather than only that one occurred; it reads indexed events only and spends no PolySwarm quota. The other three are for an AI agent reaching Splunk through an MCP server: PolySwarm Indicator Lookup answers for one indicator, the same search with Attribution adds family and actor, and PolySwarm Quota Remaining reports what is left without spending indicator quota. Two of those three spend a metered request per run, which is why enabling them is a deliberate administrative act. Every answer carries a status field reading answered, not_found, refused or error, so an automated caller never has to read English to learn whether a lookup failed or the platform holds no record. Description:
Kubernetes Search brings live, read-only access to the Kubernetes API into the Splunk search bar. Instead of switching to a terminal and kubectl, you run SPL - | k8s kind=pods namespace=payments - and Splunk queries the cluster's API server directly and streams the current state into your search. The problem it solves: when something breaks in a cluster, the question is usually "what is true right now?" - is the pod still crash-looping, what do its events say, is the node Ready. Answering that has meant leaving Splunk, holding cluster credentials, and running kubectl by hand. Ingestion pipelines give you history, but at the cost of storage and license volume, and they show the cluster only as of the last sample. Kubernetes Search answers the live question from inside Splunk, with no credentials handed out and every query recorded in the Splunk audit log. How it works: - Five search commands cover the common kubectl verbs: | k8s (list or get any resource), | k8slogs (stream pod logs), | k8sevents (cluster events), | k8sdescribe (an object plus its events), and | k8syaml (format JSON as YAML). - Everything runs on the search head and is strictly read-only - it never applies, scales, or deletes anything. - Nothing is indexed: no storage cost, no license volume, no source types, no field extractions. Results exist only for the life of your search. - Register many clusters and fan out with context=* - each row carries a cluster field, so you query and aggregate across your whole fleet from one pane. - Access is gated by a Splunk capability and a per-cluster credential model (shared, per-user, or Kubernetes impersonation), so analysts get controlled, audited read access without being handed kubectl or cluster credentials. - A short-lived on-disk cache keeps dashboards from hammering your API servers; Secrets are never cached. There is no agent to install in your cluster - only a network route from the search head to the API server and a credential. The app installs on search heads only and writes nothing to any index. It pairs naturally with ingestion: use Monitoring Kubernetes or OpenTelemetry for history and trends, and Kubernetes Search for the live picture - in the same Splunk session. The prior implementation only performed a partial join in some cases. - Merging on Investigate > Calls is now done by a new mergecalls search command, which merges whole calls, follows chains of linked calls of any length, and holds only a few hours of calls in memory at a time. - **Functionality** - New "merge across SME by session id" option on Investigate > Calls (experimental), which joins the legs of a call on either side of an SME by their RFC 7989 session ID. - **Functionality** - New "merge by ciscoguid" option on Investigate > Calls. Unlike the conversationId and session id options it is not CUCM-only: ciscoguid means the same thing on CUCM, CUBE, CVP and SBC records, so it merges a call across clusters and across technologies. - **Functionality** - In all versions of Investigate Calls prior to this release the concurrency and duration_elapsed fields were always empty for every data type except CUCM and CUBE. Both now work for all of them. - **Performance** - The Investigate > Devices page is dramatically faster, commonly 5x to 10x, and more on larger deployments, as a result of eliminating an mvexpand in the SPL. - **Performance** - Investigate > Calls, and every other search that uses the devices lookup, is commonly 2x faster or more, because that lookup no longer allows wildcards. - **Important** - A "*" in the clusterId column of the devices lookup no longer matches any cluster. A new health check lists such rows, and the new App Settings > General page can turn wildcards back on. - **Important** - A CUCM node that is upgraded or reinstalled can reuse old call ids, merging unrelated calls. A new health check finds this, and the new call_id_resets lookup keeps them apart. Each warning includes a search you can run once to record the reset. - On Investigate > Calls, legs of one call that connect in the same second are now always listed in origination order, rather than sometimes in arbitrary order. - On Investigate > Calls, a leg with no value in a text column, or in duration, no longer shifts the values below it up a row, against the wrong leg. This was most common on calls that cross CUCM, CUBE, Oracle SBC and CVP. Other numeric columns, and the CMR quality columns, are not lined up with the legs yet. - **Functionality** - The field gallery now documents the Oracle SBC CDR fields, about 230 of them, so they appear in the field picker with descriptions when Oracle SBC is selected. It also fills in 50 CUBE fields that were missing. - The home page's Explore fields panel now samples CUBE and Oracle SBC data separately from CUCM, so their fields no longer show as not in your data. Each field now also says which data types it is found in, and the search box matches on that too. - Eleven fields are now treated as numbers rather than as categories, including the CUCM audio and video bandwidth fields, CUBE's h323_voice_quality and charged_units, and the CMR's videoOneWayDelay. - The Extension, Outside Party and Huntgroup detail pages no longer mix CUBE records into some of their panels. Those panels counted a call through both CUBE and CUCM twice and disagreed with the rest of the page. For CUBE, use Investigate > Calls. - The Call Detail page now labels legs from the cube_cdr_compact sourcetype with their CUBE direction and activity, as it already did for cube_cdr. - On Investigate > Calls, selecting some but not all clusters no longer hides every CUBE, Oracle SBC and CVP leg. The cluster filters now apply only to CUCM records. - **Functionality** - CVP calls now show on Investigate > Calls with CVP selected, one leg per SIP INVITE, and join their CUCM call under "merge by ciscoguid". Needs SA_cisco_ucce 0.2.0. - **Critical** - On a Splunk Free license the app's first-time-run script never ran at all, because Splunk cannot honor passAuth = splunk-system-user there. None of the app's editable lookups were ever created. - Expanded the field gallery descriptions for the directory URI party fields. - The gallery now also notes that a directory URI whose host is an IP address is the SIP URI as signaled, which incidentally is the same form Expressway, Cisco Meeting Server and SBC records use. - Expanded the gallery descriptions for the RFC 7989 session ID fields and the IMS charging fields (ICID and the IOI pair), which are purpose-built cross- system correlators rather than addresses. - Fixed a bug in the search filters field, where a tab character preceding a field=value searchterm would be handled incorrectly triggering a parse error from splunkd. - The callquality command no longer fails the entire search when call_quality_thresholds.csv is absent. It falls back to the shipped default thresholds and warns. - The two "Other calls to/from" panels on the CUBE call detail view now show whole calls, rather than only the legs that carried one of the parties, and no longer collapse identical legs into one. - Fixed a bug where the call detail page found no CUBE legs at all for a call whose guid begins with a zero, roughly one call in sixteen. It matched the zero-padded call_reference_id against the guid text, which is not padded. - The call detail page now finds a call's CUBE legs by ciscoguid. Before, a CUBE leg reached through a CUCM trunk-to-trunk leg was missing there, even when Investigate Calls showed it. - The call detail page has its own data type selector, set from Investigate Calls, and brings in a call's records from every selected system that carries its ciscoguid: CUBE, Oracle SBC, CVP, UCCE and CCCSP. - On Investigate Calls, a call that went through CUCM and an Oracle SBC now has one "view call details" link, to the main call detail page, as CUBE calls already did. The Oracle SBC detail view remains for calls that never touched CUCM. - The call flow diagram on the call detail page now draws a call's Oracle SBC and CUBE hops alongside its CUCM legs, with each box named the way it is named in CUCM. - In the call detail page's legs table, every non-CUCM row now gets the alternate background, the note above the table names which systems those rows came from, and data_type is now a default column. - The "other data sources" panel on the call detail page now also searches the app's own indexes, and recognizes a call's ciscoguid in each of the forms those systems write it. - Fixed a bug where if you had the conversationId merging option on, CUBE and Cisco Meeting Server legs fell out of any call that merged, and showed up as a separate call carrying a CUCM call id. - The health checks for required Splunk and app versions are now one check each, covering every installed Sideview app, in place of the eight near- identical copies the apps used to ship. Six fewer searches run when the health checks page loads. - Those two checks also now work for roles without the rest_access_server_endpoints capability, where previously they failed outright rather than reporting anything. - A sourcetypes list in sideview_data_types.conf may now be comma-separated as well as space-separated. Before, a comma silently hid that data type's events. - The devices lookup health check no longer fails when extra columns have been added to the lookup. Extra columns are now reported as INFO, and only missing columns fail the check. - The call_failed field no longer counts ordinary human outcomes as failures: wrong numbers (including SIP 404, 410, 484 and 604), no answer, busy (including SIP 486 and 600), declined (603), the caller hanging up while it rang (487), answered on another phone, or a party dropped from a conference. - Calls ending in SIP 420 Bad Extension or cause 155 "DCC Allowed Percentage Exceeded" previously had no call_failed value at all. Both now count as failed calls. - New fields connected_at and disconnected_at, defined the same way on every supported data type: when each call leg connected (empty if it never did) and when it ended. - Fixed duration_elapsed showing 0 for a call that did connect, when one of its CUCM legs never connected.

Whether troubleshooting individual calls or building high level reporting, it helps you visualize and understand in all areas: agents, users, and huntgroups; concurrency and utilization; call flow; call quality; call volume; devices; failed calls; locations and sites; and audits and compliance. # Version 1.0.6 A maintenance release: a fix that matters on busy systems, a safeguard, and a small addition. It installs over 1.0.5 or 1.0.4 and keeps your inputs and settings. ## Fixed * **Change lists no longer leave changes out.** *Recent changes* on Incident Overview and the change feed on Incident Changes now list every change of every update. In 1.0.5, once the selected period held a few hundred updates, the search behind them reached Splunk's memory limit for expanding results (`mvexpand`, 500 MB by default): Splunk showed a warning and silently dropped most of the changes. The search now carries only each incident's summary fields while listing its changes. ## Improved * **Most active incidents**, on Incident Changes, shows each incident's type, EDR or XDR, like the other incident lists. ## Upgrading * **From 1.0.5:** install 1.0.6 over it and restart Splunk. There is nothing to reconfigure, and data already indexed is unaffected. * **From 1.0.4:** the same, but read the version 1.0.5 release notes first: incident collection changed in 1.0.5, and the licence volume grows. * If you edited one of the add-on's dashboards in Splunk, your edited copy replaces the add-on's own and does not receive these changes. ## Requirements Unchanged from 1.0.5: Splunk Enterprise 8.1 or later, and a GravityZone API key with access to the Incidents API (`getIncidentsList`, `getIncidentsByIds`) and the Accounts API (`getActivityLogsForCompany`).


Short Description:
Collects Bitdefender GravityZone security incidents (EDR and XDR) and the complete console activity log into Splunk. Every change to an incident is indexed with a readable summary of what changed, console actions on incidents are linked to the incidents they affected, and four dashboards cover triage, incident history, response times and ingestion health.


Description:
Bitdefender GravityZone Data Collector brings GravityZone security incidents and console activity into Splunk. GravityZone incidents do not stand still: alerts are added, more endpoints become involved, severity changes, and analysts assign, prioritise, comment on and close them. The add-on collects that whole history, so you can triage, investigate and report on GravityZone incidents alongside the rest of your security data. It collects two kinds of data through the GravityZone API, one input per GravityZone company, so a single Splunk deployment can follow many companies, as partners and managed service providers need. The first is security incidents, both endpoint (EDR) and extended (XDR): every time an incident changes, the add-on indexes the new version with a field-level diff and a short, readable summary of what changed. The second is console activity: every entry of the company's GravityZone user activity log, such as sign-ins and failed sign-ins, changes to users and companies, tasks, quarantine actions and actions on incidents, each indexed as its own searchable event. Actions on incidents are also linked to the incidents they affected. Four dashboards are included. Incident Overview shows what is open, how serious it is, who owns it, who initiated it and what GravityZone did about it. Incident Changes is a filterable feed of changes, with severity and priority escalations and re-opened incidents. Incident Detail shows the current state and full history of one incident, with its alerts, nodes and notes, the incidents GravityZone grouped with it, and who changed it in the console. SLA and Ingestion Health shows the time taken to assign and to resolve incidents, open work by owner, and whether every input is collecting. The dashboards focus on incidents; the complete console activity log is available to your own searches, selected by gz_event_type=activity_log. All data uses the bitdefender:gravityzone sourcetype, with plain summary fields named gz_* that keep your own searches simple and fast.

item.description:

Release Notes:
To keep **searches responsive** over large modules (e.g. `logarchive`), the Addon extracts a selected set of high-value fields at **index time** for the `digit:saf:parseddata:json` source type only. These fields are stored in the index and and bring a massive performance gain when searching. The index-time fields are prefixed with `saf_idx_` (underscores only) so their names are unique, valid as indexed field keys, and never collide with the search-time `KV_MODE = json` fields. The original (un-prefixed, dotted) names remain available at search time via `KV_MODE = json`, but don't benefit from the speed. **For a given field you therefore have two names: use the `saf_idx_` name for fast filtering and `| tstats`, and the plain name (e.g. `data.process`) for everything else.** Indexed fields (12): `saf_idx_module`, `saf_idx_case_id`, `saf_idx_timestamp_desc`, `saf_idx_data_event_type`, `saf_idx_data_log_type`, `saf_idx_data_euid`, `saf_idx_data_boot_uuid`, `saf_idx_data_process`, `saf_idx_data_pid`, `saf_idx_data_subsystem`, `saf_idx_data_category`, `saf_idx_data_library`. Notes: * **Filtering** on an indexed field is faster transparently (e.g. `saf_idx_data_process=mussel`). **Aggregating** fast requires `| tstats` (e.g. `| tstats count by saf_idx_data_process`); a `search ... | stats` still scans raw events. Trailing wildcards (`keyword*`) use the index; leading wildcards (`*keyword`) do not. * Index-time fields apply only to data indexed **after** this config is in place. To benefit on existing cases, perform a one-time clean + reingest. New cases get the fields automatically. * **Scope:** because the indexed names carry the `saf_idx_` prefix, they are unique to this TA. `fields.conf` (`INDEXED = true`) applies only to these `saf_idx_*` names, so it does not affect the plain `KV_MODE = json` fields or any unrelated data on the same instance.


Description:
EC DIGIT CSIRC Add-on for Sysdiagnose Analysis Framework (SAF) is a Splunk Technical Addon designed to facilitate the collection and processing of the artefacts generated by the Sysdiagnose Analysis Framework (SAF). This addon provides a set of configurations and scripts to streamline data ingestion and ensure proper handling within the Splunk environment.

Release Notes:
Version 2.0.0 2.0.0 is a major release. It changes the event format, so read "Upgrading from 1.1.x" before you upgrade. NEW * Cyber feeds: the input now also collects Luminar finished intelligence reports and the threat actors, campaigns, malware, vulnerabilities (CVEs), targeted sectors and locations they cover. * New event format: one JSON event per STIX object, with ready-to-use IOC fields (ioc\_type, ioc\_value, ip, domain, url, file\_hash, email), the feed name (luminar\_feed) and Luminar context such as luminar.score. * Lookups: ten saved searches build lookups after each collection. They include active IOCs (KV Store) with expiry and a minimum score (luminar\_min\_score macro, default 60), IOC attribution to threat actors and malware, report context, a domain lookup that also matches subdomains, CVE intelligence with Luminar exploitation flags and CVSS, and leaked accounts. * Detection rules: six correlation searches, shipped disabled. They cover connections to malicious IPs, web requests to malicious URLs, malicious file hashes on endpoints, DNS queries to malicious domains and their subdomains, successful logins by leaked accounts, and scanner CVEs that Luminar reports on. * They read the CIM data models by default; each rule's log-source macro can point it at your own data instead. * In Splunk Enterprise Security they appear as correlation searches, with the notable event settings already filled in. * Alert history: the detection rules write every alert to the luminar\_alerts index. The new Detection Matches dashboard shows them by rule, severity, threat actor, malware and affected asset. * Allowlist: stop alerts on known false positives, such as CDN IP addresses or test accounts, for all rules or one rule, with an expiry date and a reason. * New dashboards: Threat Intel Overview, Threat Profiles, Leaked Credentials, Cyberfeeds, Luminar Report, Ingest Health, Detection Matches, Allowlist and Log Sources. The Main Dashboard adds cyber feeds panels and an ingest-time filter. * Field menu actions: look up an IP address, domain, URL, file hash, account or CVE in Luminar from any search result, and open threat actor, malware and campaign profiles and reports. * New input settings: * "Mask Leaked Passwords", on by default: leaked passwords keep only their first and last character, and the clear text is never written to Splunk. * "Rebuild Lookups After Collection", on by default. * Credentials are checked when an input is saved. If Luminar rejects them, or the host cannot be reached, the input is not saved and the reason is shown on the form. CHANGES AND FIXES * Each feed keeps its own checkpoint, so an interrupted run resumes from its last batch. * Indicators that have already expired when they are collected are no longer ingested. * Deleting an input also deletes its checkpoints, so an input re-created with the same name starts from its initial fetch date. * Searches, lookups and the new dashboards read the Luminar index through the luminar\_index macro (default: index\=main). UPGRADING FROM 1.1.x 1. Review your own searches, reports and alerts on Luminar data. Events are now one per STIX object, with new field names (for example, indicator\_type is now ioc\_type). Events collected by 1.1.x keep their old format. 2. If your input writes to an index other than main, set the luminar\_index macro to that index (Settings > Advanced search > Search macros). 3. Existing inputs continue from their 1.1.x checkpoint; you do not need to re-create them. The new cyber feeds start from the same point. 4. The lookups and dashboards fill after the first collection that follows the upgrade. To build them sooner, run the saved searches "Luminar - 01" to "Luminar - 10" in order. 5. To use the detection rules: a. Create the luminar\_alerts index. b. Point the rules' log-source macros at your data (the Log Sources dashboard tests them). c. Enable the rules. See "Detection rules" in the README. REQUIREMENTS * Splunk Enterprise with Python 3.13 (tested on Splunk Enterprise 10.6), with the KV Store enabled. * Optional, for the detection rules as shipped: the Splunk Common Information Model add-on and CIM-mapped data. Support: this add-on is developer supported by Cognyte. Contact [luminar@cognyte.com](mailto:luminar@cognyte.com).

A Splunk® Add-On providing the custom search commands cipher, crypt, encode, and hash for ciphering/deciphering, encrypting/decrypting, encoding/decoding and hashing fields and events at search time. * Cipher/decipher fields or complete events during search time using RC4, ROT13, ROT47, XOR * Encrypt/decrypt fields or complete events during search time using RSA, AES-128/192/256-CBC or AES-128/192/256-OFB * Encode/decode fields or complete events during search time using Base32, Base58, Base62, Base64, Binary, Decimal, Hex, Octal * Hash fields or complete events during search time using MD5, SHA1, SHA2 (224, 256, 384, 512), SHA3 (224, 256, 384, 512), Blake2 * Manage access to encryption and decryption functionality on a per-user or per-role basis via two shipped roles * Manage usable encryption/decryption keys on a per-user or per-role basis via the app's configuration screen Cross-compatible with Python 2 and 3.
